blocks.heading: What the 2026 Numbers Actually Say
rows: Sector revenue, FY26
USD 315 billion, up 6.1% (Nasscom Strategic Review, 24 February 2026).
The industry is still growing. The money is not the problem.
Direct jobs, FY26
59.5 lakh people, up by about 1.35 lakh, which is 2.3% (Nasscom, same release).
Jobs grew at well under half the pace of revenue. More work is being done per person.
Five largest IT services firms, FY26
Combined headcount fell by 7,389 after a gain of 12,718 in FY25 (IANS, 25 April 2026). One other outlet counts 6,981, so the exact figure varies by source.
The big services names are no longer a guaranteed ramp for every graduate.
Fresher plans at the largest firms
TCS plans about 25,000 freshers in FY27, against 40,000 to 42,000 in earlier years. Infosys expects about 20,000 (IANS, 25 April 2026).
Seats exist, but fewer than the batch before you expected.
Global capability centres (GCCs)
About 2,117 centres and 2.36 million people in FY26 (Zinnov report, reported 19 August 2026).
The fastest-growing employers prefer people who already have some experience.

blocks.heading: Doors In, and the Experience Entry Requirement
rows: Campus placement
The college invites firms. You are shortlisted on marks, a test and an interview.
Depends on your college. Weak campuses may see few or no big-firm visits.
Company tests off campus
Large firms run open hiring tests for graduates from many colleges and courses. Check the company page for the current course, batch and marks rules before you apply.
Thousands compete for each seat, so a test score alone rarely stands out.
Referral and direct application
A current employee passes your profile on, or you apply with proof of work.
Needs a network and a visible project. Most freshers skip building both.
Lateral move after experience
You move from one employer to a better one after you have real delivery on your record.
This is the door GCCs and product firms prefer. You must clear the first job to reach it.

blocks.heading: Routes Ranked By How Far They Scale
rows: Build a skill portfolio, then sell it directly (freelance or small consulting)
Scalable
You set the price, add clients, and can later hire or package the work. Web, data, automation, testing and security skills all sell this way.
Needs a business layer: a clear offer, proof, referrals and a price conversation. See the section on who pays.
Product company, GCC or startup engineering, data, cloud or security role
Scalable
The skills carry across employers and can grow into specialist or lead roles, and into consulting later.
Hard to enter straight after college because GCCs lean toward experienced hires. Plan it as the second job.
Own a small IT services or product business
Scalable
You own the pricing and the customer list, and software can serve many customers.
High risk. It works best after you have a skill, a few paying clients and a few years of delivery.
Salaried IT services role (development, testing, business analysis, ERP)
Scalable with a business layer
Stable first income and client exposure, but pay follows a fixed grade ladder.
The layer is your own: turn the experience into a specialist lane, consulting or a move to product.
Support, service desk and BPM roles
Not so scalable
Routine, ticket-based work with a low ceiling and heavy automation pressure.
Useful as a paid bridge into testing, cloud operations, security operations or analysis. Do not stay passive here.

blocks.heading: Not a CS Graduate
rows: BCA or BSc (IT, CS, maths, physics, electronics)
Large firms have accepted these degrees in open hiring tests. These rules change by year, so confirm on the company page.
Development, testing, support moving to cloud or security operations.
BCom, BA or BBA
Direct coding jobs are harder to reach. The better doors are business analysis, ERP or finance-systems functional roles, testing, and BPM that you use as a bridge.
Business analyst, techno-functional consultant, data analyst, product operations.
Non-CS engineer (mechanical, civil, electrical, chemical)
You can enter IT services through tests, but your branch is an asset in engineering R&D, simulation, automation and data work for your own industry.
Domain plus data, or domain plus software. Read the non-CS engineers guide.
Diploma holder or Class 12 pass
Possible through skills first: a clear portfolio, an internship or small client work. A degree is not legally required for most IT work, but many employers filter on it.
Web, testing, support to cloud operations, freelance projects.

blocks.heading: Who Should Skip
rows: You want a job that is safe because of the company name
In FY26 the five largest services firms together cut headcount. Safety now comes from a skill other employers want, not from a logo.
You dislike learning new tools every year
Tools, clients and AI methods keep changing. The people who stall are usually the ones who stopped learning, not the ones who lacked talent.
You cannot handle repetitive work for the first stretch
Most first jobs include ticket work, testing cycles or support queues. If that will crush you, choose an analysis or design-led door instead.
You want fast, large pay straight after college
The large offers go to a small slice. Most people start modestly and grow through a second move, not the first offer.
You are choosing IT only because relatives say it pays well
That was a stronger argument when the entry ramp was wider. Test your interest with a small build before you commit years.

blocks.heading: Start, By Situation
rows: Class 12 student choosing a course

Compare BCA, BSc and B.Tech by what the college proves, not its name. Keep to roughly 10% of the family education budget for the degree and keep the rest for laptop, internet, projects and learning. Build one small project before you pay any fees.
Final-year student or fresher
Take the first paid role if it gives structure, but write down the second job now: product, GCC, analysis, security or cloud. Start the portfolio in the first month of work, not in the third year.
Working in support or testing
Use the Ladder or Treadmill check. Move toward automation, cloud operations or security operations while you are still employed.
Mid-career in a services firm
Do not wait for the next appraisal to decide for you. Build a specialist lane, a visible proof asset and outside contacts, then look at GCC, product or consulting.
Not in IT, thinking of switching
Pick the nearest door from your current domain, such as analysis, domain testing or functional ERP. Do not start with a full coding reset unless you enjoy it.

visuals.heading: IT Services Trap

items.text: Same type of ticket for three years, only faster.
Skills that match one client's internal tools.
No work you can show outside the company.
A raise cycle that pays a fixed small step.
Positioning: say who you help and with what, in one sentence.
Proof: one live demo, one small case note, one referral they can check.
First skill to learn: a simple offer and a calm price conversation.
One number to watch: how many conversations turn into paid trial work.
